clue.text: Put silver in vessels for heathens

indicators.note: to put something is to place it somewhere, and the place is named by the word that follows
'in' names that place as the inside of what comes next

blocks.note: pans are the vessels of a kitchen
ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from Latin argentum

explanation.surface: Silver is being loaded into the cooking pots for people outside the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Silver is the chemist's AG far more often than it is anything else in a cryptic. The churchy surface makes 'heathens' look like scene-setting rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pagans are people outside the main religions, and heathen is the older, harsher word for exactly that.

clue.text: Agent upset by thousand as bonus

indicators.note: something upset has been tipped over, and in a down entry that means it reads back up the column

blocks.note: a rep is an agent, the one who calls on the shops, and here the word is turned round
k = thousand, the k of a thirty-k salary

explanation.surface: An agent is put out by a bonus of a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' can only mean reversed in a down clue; the same setter would need a different word going across. K for thousand comes from kilo, and British pay is quoted in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A perk is the extra a job hands you on top of the wages, which is what a bonus is.

clue.text: Vessel volume written across bottom of base

indicators.note: writing across something lays your line over the top of it, so one word ends up spanning the other
the bottom of a word is the letter it finishes on

blocks.note: a gallon is a volume, the old British measure of eight pints
the last letter of basE

explanation.surface: The capacity of a container is stamped across the foot of its base.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the surface talk about holding liquid, so 'vessel' reads as a jug rather than a ship. A measure hidden inside a word for a ship is the sort of pairing a setter hunts for.
explanation.definitionFit: A galleon is a big square-rigged sailing ship, and 'vessel' is the standard word for anything that floats.

clue.text: Declared info edit mistakenly

indicators.note: anything done mistakenly comes out wrong, and letters that come out wrong are not in the order they were given

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A press office announces a change to its information by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder sits in plain sight as two ordinary words with nothing odd about them, which is why the indicator is the only clue to what is happening. 'Declared' is the official sense, as in a notifiable disease.
explanation.definitionFit: To notify is to announce something officially, the same sense as declaring goods at customs.

clue.text: Joker retaining European system regularly getting fondled

indicators.note: to retain something is to keep hold of it inside you, so one word closes round another
taking a word regularly means picking its letters at a steady interval, every other one

blocks.note: the joker is a card, and a card is also the old word for a joker in the sense of a wag
e = European
the first, third and fifth letters of SySTeM

explanation.surface: A comic who sticks to the European way of doing things is regularly petted for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joker' splits after three of its four letters to take in everything else, so 'retaining' has a lot to hold. Counting 'regularly' from the first letter rather than the second is what makes the S turn up twice.
explanation.definitionFit: To caress someone is to stroke them fondly, which is what fondled says in one word.

clue.text: Paid choirs off with a stimulant

indicators.note: to go off is to turn, and letters that have turned no longer sit in the order given

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
the clue's own 'a', joined to the fodder to make eleven

explanation.surface: The choirs were paid off in something livelier than cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paid off' is a phrase the surface needs whole, so the instruction hides in the second half of it. The small 'a' has to be swept up as well, which is easy to miss when counting.
explanation.definitionFit: An aphrodisiac is taken to rouse desire, so it stimulates — the definition names the effect without naming the appetite.

clue.text: Fake emerald ring sold as turquoise zirconia originally

indicators.note: what a word is originally is the letter it starts out with

blocks.clueFragment: emerald ring sold as turquoise zirconia
blocks.note: the initials of the six words, in the order given

explanation.surface: A jeweller offers an emerald ring sold as turquoise and zirconia.
explanation.walkthrough: Six initials in a row is a long run, and the tell is that the list is all gemstones and settings — too tidy to be chance. 'Originally' has to reach back across the whole clue to do its work.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz is German for 'replacement', and in English it always means a poor substitute passed off as the real thing.

clue.text: Nieces upset about constant Physics?

indicators.note: something upset has been knocked over, and letters knocked over land in a new order
when one thing goes about another it passes round the outside of it

blocks.note: the six letters of NIECES in another order, opening after the first to take one more
c = constant, the algebraist's stand-in for a fixed number

explanation.surface: The nieces are worked up over a constant in their physics homework.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: it warns that the definition names one branch of a wider thing rather than the thing itself. C for constant comes straight out of the algebra lesson the surface is set in.
explanation.definitionFit: Physics is one of the sciences, so this is definition by example, and the question mark is the setter owning up to it.

clue.text: We hear smart cat weed

indicators.note: 'we hear' asks you to listen to the words rather than read them, so the spelling is free to change

blocks.note: a dandy is a smart dresser, and said aloud the word can be spelt this way instead
a lion is a big cat

explanation.surface: Word reaches us of a smartly turned-out cat out among the weeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words is all the setter needs, because the whole joke is that two of them said together sound like a third thing. The plant's name really does come from the French dent-de-lion, lion's tooth, for its jagged leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A dandelion is the yellow-flowered plant that colonises lawns, and 'weed' is the gardener's word for it.

clue.text: Report about dead

blocks.note: re = about, the 'concerning' at the head of a memo
the late Mr So-and-so is the dead one

explanation.surface: News is coming in about somebody who has died.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of the commonest crossword pieces there are, laid end to end in six letters. 'Report' is the verb — to recount — and not the document the surface is offering.
explanation.definitionFit: To relate an event is to report it, the storyteller's sense of the word rather than the newsroom's.

clue.text: Article: spread covering one performer

indicators.note: to cover something is to lie right over the top of it, keeping it underneath

blocks.note: 'the' is the definite article
a span is the spread of a bridge or of a pair of wings
i = one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A magazine article gives its double-page spread over to a single performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' in a cryptic is nearly always the grammar word, THE or A, rather than something you read. The colon keeps the newspaper picture going long enough to hide that.
explanation.definitionFit: A thespian is an actor, the lofty word for one, after Thespis who is said to have stepped out of the Greek chorus first.

clue.text: Policeman frets about egotism

indicators.note: 'about' is the roughly of about-a-dozen, and a rough copy of some letters need not keep them in order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: A policeman is fretting over somebody's swollen ego.
explanation.walkthrough: A fourteen-letter anagram across the middle of the grid is usually the way in, and the 4-10 enumeration tells you where the hyphen lands. 'About' is the quiet instruction here: it means roughly, not around.
explanation.definitionFit: Egotism and the answer both name an inflated sense of your own worth; egotism is the bookish word for it.

clue.text: Claim ritual involved embracing people of all origins

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up in itself, and tangled letters have lost the order they came in

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A club claims its initiation ritual welcomes people of every background.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embracing' looks like a container instruction and is not — it opens the definition, which runs to the last five words. Only 'involved' asks you to move anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A multiracial society is made up of people of many races, so it takes in all origins at once.

clue.text: Cut sore hip area

blocks.note: a tender spot is a sore one
the loins are the part of the body at the hips and lower back

explanation.surface: A surgeon cuts into a sore patch at the hip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a verb doing something to the sore hip, and it is a noun — the butcher's word for a piece of meat. Wordplay and definition end up describing the same anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenderloin is a cut of beef or pork taken from the loin, so 'cut' is the butcher's noun for it.

clue.text: Tickle bird getting sick and annoyed

blocks.note: a tit is a small garden bird, blue or great
sick and ill are the same complaint
to eat at someone is to nag or worry them — what's eating you? — so annoyed is ate

explanation.surface: Somebody tickles a bird that has fallen sick, and annoys it.
explanation.walkthrough: ATE for 'annoyed' is the awkward step, leaning on the colloquial 'eat' that means to gnaw away at someone. The bird is the crossword regular, three letters and always the same one.
explanation.definitionFit: To titillate is to tickle, first in the literal sense and then in the sense of tickling somebody's interest.

clue.text: Snowman is even icier at first

indicators.note: what a word is at first is the single letter it opens with

blocks.note: 'even colder' and 'yet colder' say the same thing, so even is yet
the first letter of Icier

explanation.surface: Tonight is turning out even icier than the last one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' is so often the alternate-letters instruction that a solver reaches for that first; here it is a plain synonym. 'Snowman' is capitalised only because it opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti is the abominable snowman of Himalayan report, so the definition is the creature's other name.

clue.text: Infallible fellow having trouble with vault

blocks.note: f = fellow, the F of FRS after an academic's name
to ail is to be in trouble, the verb behind an ailing business
a bank's vault is its safe

explanation.surface: A chap in difficulty is struggling with the vault at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vault' pulls straight towards the gymnasium, and the strongroom is what is wanted. The 4-4 enumeration splits the answer in a different place from the wordplay, which is why the pieces do not line up with the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: A fail-safe device cannot go wrong, because it drops into a harmless state if it does — which is the claim infallible makes.

clue.text: Make disapproving noise encountering uniform skirt that’s short

blocks.note: tut is the click of the tongue that says you disapprove
u = uniform in the radio alphabet, after tango and victor

explanation.surface: A teacher clicks her tongue at a uniform whose skirt has been taken up too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' does both jobs at once: the clothing the surface needs and the radio alphabet's letter. The definition describes the garment rather than naming the dance it belongs to.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutu is the short stiff skirt a ballerina dances in, so 'skirt that's short' describes it exactly.

clue.text: Skill granted after time to make little pastry

indicators.note: coming after something means coming behind it, and in a down entry behind means further down the column

blocks.note: t = time, the T of a countdown's T-minus
art is skill — the art of conversation is the knack of it
a flat granted to a tenant is let to them

explanation.surface: Time and practice grant the skill needed for a small pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is the whole reason the time goes first, so it is an instruction and not just a join. 'Granted' is the landlord's sense of let, which is the step most solvers have to go back for.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartlet is a small individual tart, the -let ending doing the work of 'little'.

clue.text: Left copy showing lack of talent

blocks.note: l = left, as on a map key or a signpost
an imitation is a copy of the real thing

explanation.surface: The copy somebody left behind shows how little talent they had.
explanation.walkthrough: One letter plus one long word is as simple as a charade gets, so the work is all in spotting where the definition starts. 'Left' reads as the past tense of leave and is the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's limitations are the things they have not the talent for, so a limitation is a lack of talent.

clue.text: Domestic chore I call about in advance

indicators.note: when one thing goes about another it wraps round the outside of it

blocks.note: the clue's own I, taken as a letter
to call somebody is to ring them
to advance is to move on, so what is in advance is on

explanation.surface: I phone ahead about who is doing the housework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' is a letter of the answer, not the setter talking about themselves, and it is sitting there in capitals to make you think otherwise. The chore is the definition, parked at the front where an ordinary noun phrase can hide.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironing is the household job of pressing clothes, a domestic chore by anyone's reckoning.

clue.text: Clears revolting instrument for removing tartar

indicators.note: to revolt is to rise up against the established order, and letters in revolt abandon the order they were put in

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A stomach-turning tool at the dentist's clears the muck off your teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' means in revolt, not disgusting, though the dental surface works hard for the other reading. The definition takes the whole second half and describes the tool instead of naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A scaler is the dentist's hooked pick for scraping tartar off teeth, scale being the old name for that hard deposit.

clue.text: Minister in cold hall corner shivering

indicators.note: something shivering is shaking all over, and shaken letters do not stay where they were put

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Somebody is shivering in the cold corner of a hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Counting is the way in: the clue has exactly fourteen letters to spare once the first word and the last are set aside. 'In' is only a join, though it reads as part of the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Chancellor is the British cabinet minister answerable for the courts and the judiciary, so this is definition by example.

clue.text: Leader with unpleasant odour starts to smell sweeter

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it opens with, and two words asked for their starts give a letter each

blocks.note: BO is body odour, the two letters British advertising made unmentionable
the opening letters of Smell and Sweeter

explanation.surface: The man in charge has begun to smell rather sweeter than he did.
explanation.walkthrough: BO turns up in cryptics far more often than in conversation, and it is always worth trying when a clue mentions a smell. 'Starts' is plural for a reason: two words are being asked, not one.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is whoever is in charge of a workplace, which is what a leader is.

clue.text: Everyone the Spanish united beginning to intone a song of praise

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is the letter it sets off with

blocks.note: everyone is all of them
el is the Spanish for 'the'
u = united, the U of a football club's name
the first letter of Intone
the clue's own 'a', taken at face value

explanation.surface: The whole congregation and the Spanish join in as the hymn begins.
explanation.walkthrough: Five pieces for eight letters, three of them single letters, which is the shape of a charade rather than anything cleverer. The last 'a' belongs to the wordplay, not to the definition it seems to introduce.
explanation.definitionFit: Alleluia is the shout of praise sung in church, the Hebrew for 'praise the Lord' left untranslated.

clue.text: Piece of radical, iconoclastic material

indicators.note: a piece of something is part of it taken whole, and what is taken whole here is a run of letters

blocks.note: hiding across the join: radiCAL, ICOnoclastic

explanation.surface: Somebody is describing a piece of radical, image-smashing art.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is the disguise — the hidden run crosses it as though the punctuation were not there. 'Piece of' is a standard flag for letters lifted out of the clue untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: Calico is a plain cotton cloth named after Calicut in India, and cloth is material.

clue.text: Completely new exhaust after rear of vehicle loudly evacuated

indicators.note: 'after' means later along the line, so whatever it points back to has to be written down first
the rear of a word is the letter at the end of it
a building that has been evacuated has nobody left in the middle, only what stands at each end

blocks.note: the last letter of vehiclE
n = new
to exhaust somebody is to tire them
LoudlY with its middle cleared out, leaving the two letters at the ends

explanation.surface: A completely new exhaust goes on after the back of the car was noisily cleared out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust' is the verb, to tire someone, while the surface keeps it a car part throughout. 'Loudly' looks like a homophone flag and is instead a word to be emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: Entirely and completely are both adverbs meaning in full, with no part of it left out.

clue.text: Tightly packs shoes

blocks.note: the verb: to jam something hard into a space
the noun: footwear built on a solid sloping heel

explanation.surface: Someone crams a case of shoes as tight as it will go.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-word clue is nearly always two definitions stood side by side, since there is no room for anything else. 'Shoes' looks like the object of the verb and is a definition in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: To wedge something is to pack it tightly into a gap; wedges are also shoes whose heel and sole are one solid sloping block.
